prompt: Before asking anybody, pc1's `ip route` printed nothing at all. What does that tell you?
hint: An empty table has no line for anything.

choices.text: It has no IPv4 route, not even to its own subnet
choices.why: Right. Without an address there is no subnet route either, and no gateway.

choices.text: It has a default route that `ip route` hides
choices.why: When pc1 has one, `ip route` prints it on the first line, as it does after the DHCP exchange.

choices.text: Its fe80 address gives it a route to r1
choices.why: fe80:: is IPv6 link-local; this is the IPv4 table, and it is empty.

choices.text: The cable is unplugged
choices.why: `ip -br addr` showed eth0 UP. The link is there; the address is not.

prompt: Which machine in the lab has to keep a static address?
hint: Think about who would answer if it asked for one.

choices.text: prn, the printer everybody prints to
choices.why: It has a reservation instead: the same address, still asked for by DHCP.

choices.text: srv, the DHCP server
choices.why: Right. It cannot lease an address to itself before it is running.

choices.text: pc4, because it is on another subnet
choices.why: pc4 gets its address by DHCP, through the relay on r1.

choices.text: pc1, because it asked first
choices.why: Asking first only decides which pool address it gets: .100.

prompt: After its DHCP exchange, what had pc1 been given by the server? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read `ip -br addr`, `ip route` and `/etc/resolv.conf` after the ACK.

choices.text: An address with its mask, 10.20.10.100/24
choices.why: Right, and the mask gave it the route to its subnet.

choices.text: A default gateway, 10.20.10.1
choices.why: Right: `default via 10.20.10.1`, from `option routers`.

choices.text: A name server, 10.20.10.10
choices.why: Right: written into /etc/resolv.conf.

choices.text: Its MAC address, 02:25:70:bc:29:c6
choices.why: The MAC belongs to the network card, and the client sent it in the request.

choices.text: The switch port it is plugged into
choices.why: DHCP knows nothing about ports; the switch does.

prompt: Put the four messages of pc1 getting its address in the order they were sent.
hint: Its initials spell a word.
items: DHCPACK, and pc1 binds the address
trap: A REQUEST before the OFFER is the usual slip: the client cannot ask for an address nobody has offered yet.

prompt: In srv's tcpdump, pc1's two messages leave from 0.0.0.0 port 68. Why 0.0.0.0?
hint: What did `ip -br addr` show before the exchange?

choices.text: It is the DHCP server's listening address
choices.why: srv is 10.20.10.10, and the messages are going TO it, not from it.

choices.text: dhclient hides the real address
choices.why: There is no real address to hide: pc1 has no IPv4 address yet.

choices.text: pc1 has no IPv4 address yet
choices.why: Right. All zeros is "no address", the only honest source it has.

choices.text: It is the broadcast address of 10.20.10.0/24
choices.why: That would be 10.20.10.255; the messages go to 255.255.255.255.

prompt: pc1 already knows from the offer which server answered. Why does it still broadcast its DHCPREQUEST?
hint: Imagine two servers on the subnet.

choices.text: So that every server that offered learns which offer was taken
choices.why: Right. The others take their addresses back.

choices.text: Because a server listens on 255.255.255.255 and nowhere else
choices.why: srv receives unicast too: the release in the leases section went straight to 10.20.10.10.

choices.text: Because it does not know the server's MAC
choices.why: The offer arrived in a frame from the server's MAC, so it knows it.

choices.text: So the router learns the new address
choices.why: r1 is not part of the exchange on the office LAN.

prompt: DHCP runs over UDP. The server listens on port 67, and the client on port ___.
hint: One more than the server.

prompt: srv's scope for the office says `range 10.20.10.100 10.20.10.199`. How many addresses can it lend?
hint: Both ends are included.

prompt: A technician gives a new access point the static address 10.20.10.150 on this lab's office LAN. What is wrong?
hint: Compare .150 with the configuration.

choices.text: .150 is in the pool, so srv could lend it to a PC as well
choices.why: Right. Two machines would then claim one address.
The /24 runs from .0 to .255; .150 is inside it.

choices.text: An access point needs a reservation to work
choices.why: A static address works; this one is just in the wrong place.

choices.text: r1 drops traffic from addresses above .99
choices.why: r1 routes the whole /24; the .99 line is only a habit of this lab.

prompt: What does `option routers 10.20.10.1;` inside the first subnet block give each client?
hint: Look at pc1's `ip route` after the exchange.

choices.text: The address of the DHCP server
choices.why: That is srv, 10.20.10.10, sent as the server identifier.

choices.text: Its default gateway
choices.why: Right: `default via 10.20.10.1`.

choices.text: The first address of the pool
choices.why: The pool is the `range` line and starts at .100.

choices.text: A router to ask for a second opinion
choices.why: DHCP has no such thing; routers is the gateway option.

prompt: How does srv know that the machine asking is the printer, and owed 10.20.10.50?
hint: Read the `host prn` block.

choices.text: Its hostname, prn
choices.why: The block is named prn for people; the match is on the hardware line.

choices.text: The switch port, p3
choices.why: srv never learns the port.

choices.text: Its MAC address, 02:32:ed:ce:04:12
choices.why: Right: `hardware ethernet` is what is matched.

choices.text: The order in which the machines ask
choices.why: Order decides the pool addresses, not a reservation.

prompt: The printer's network card is replaced, and nobody edits srv's file. What does the printer get next time it asks?
hint: What is the reservation tied to?

choices.text: 10.20.10.50, because srv knows it by its name
choices.why: The match is on the MAC address, and that changed.

choices.text: An ordinary address from the pool
choices.why: Right. The new MAC matches no host block, so it is a client like any other.

choices.text: No address at all
choices.why: An unknown MAC is simply a new client, and the pool has room.

choices.text: 10.20.10.50, kept on the printer itself
choices.why: With a reservation, the address lives in srv's file.

prompt: Why is the reserved address, 10.20.10.50, outside the pool of .100 to .199?
hint: What would happen if it were .150 and a PC asked first?

choices.text: Because dhcpd refuses reservations above .99
choices.why: Nothing in the file sets such a limit; keeping it out of the pool is a choice.

choices.text: So that it shows people the device is a printer
choices.why: An address says nothing about the device.

choices.text: Because addresses below .100 are faster
choices.why: Every address in the subnet is reached the same way.

choices.text: So that no PC is lent it before the printer asks
choices.why: Right. Outside the pool, it is never in the server's list of addresses to lend.

prompt: srv's lease file says pc1's lease starts at 11:20:32 and ends at 11:30:32. How many seconds is the lease?
hint: The configuration says it too.

prompt: A lease lasts 3600 seconds. By the protocol's default of seven eighths, how many seconds after the start does the client rebind?
hint: Seven eighths of the lease.

prompt: Match each moment in the life of a lease to what the client does.
hint: Two of them ask; one gives up; one gives back.

pairs.right: Asks the server that lent it, by unicast

right_distractors: Asks the router for a new mask

prompt: A laptop with a one-day lease is unplugged without releasing it. When is its address free for somebody else?
hint: What does an unplugged laptop send?

choices.text: At once, as soon as it stops answering
choices.why: The server does not watch for silence; it waits for the lease.

choices.text: When the day is over and the lease expires
choices.why: Right. Nothing was released, so the loan runs its course.

choices.text: At half a day, at the time it would have renewed
choices.why: Missing a renewal changes nothing on the server.

choices.text: When the server is restarted
choices.why: The leases are in a file, and a restart reads them back.

prompt: Before dhcrelay ran on r1, pc4's three DISCOVERs got no answer. Why?
hint: Where does a broadcast stop?

choices.text: srv's file had no scope for pc4's subnet, 10.20.20.0
choices.why: It did: the second subnet block.

choices.text: r1 does not forward pc4's broadcasts to the office
choices.why: Right. A router ends a broadcast domain.

choices.text: pc4's cable was unplugged
choices.why: The same cable carried the exchange a minute later.

choices.text: pc4 was using the wrong port
choices.why: Port 67, as every DISCOVER line says.

prompt: The relay writes its own address on the client's subnet into a field of the request, and the server uses it to choose the scope. That field is called ___.
hint: Its name stands for the gateway's IP address.

prompt: srv's tcpdump shows the relayed requests arriving from 10.20.10.1, and the replies going to 10.20.20.1. Why not reply to 10.20.10.1?
hint: Which of r1's addresses tells srv where the client is?

choices.text: srv replies to the giaddr the relay wrote
choices.why: Right. 10.20.20.1 is r1's address on pc4's side, and it also picked the scope.

choices.text: srv takes the reply address from `option routers`
choices.why: Here the two happen to be the same address; the reply follows the giaddr.

choices.text: 10.20.10.1 does not accept UDP
choices.why: It does: the relay sends from 10.20.10.1 port 67.

choices.text: pc4 asked for the replies to go there
choices.why: pc4 has no address yet, and no say in it.

prompt: With srv paused, pc2 took 10.20.10.200 from 10.20.10.66. Why could it then not ping 10.20.20.1?
hint: Read pc2's `ip route` before the ping.

choices.text: 10.20.10.200 is outside the office subnet
choices.why: It is inside 10.20.10.0/24, with the right mask.

choices.text: srv was paused, so the network stopped
choices.why: srv is not on the path from pc2 to r1.

choices.text: Its default route pointed at rogue, which does not route
choices.why: Right: `default via 10.20.10.66`, and nothing there forwards packets.

choices.text: The rogue gave it the wrong mask
choices.why: The connected route is 10.20.10.0/24, as before.

prompt: In the lab's snooping rule, why is p4 the port whose server messages are let through?
hint: Look at the drawing of the lab.

choices.text: p4 is the uplink to the router r1
choices.why: r1 is on p8.

choices.text: rogue is on p4
choices.why: rogue is on p5, and its offers are the ones dropped.

choices.text: srv is plugged into p4
choices.why: Right. It is the one port where a real server lives.

choices.text: nftables lets the lowest port through
choices.why: The rule names p4 itself: `iifname != "p4"`.

prompt: What does DHCP snooping on a switch do? Choose all that apply.
hint: It works on ports and on who may send what.

choices.text: Drops offers and ACKs that arrive on an untrusted port
choices.why: Right: server messages from the wrong place.

choices.text: Trusts the port towards the real server
choices.why: Right, and in the lab that is p4.

choices.text: Checks that the real server's configuration is correct
choices.why: The switch sees messages, not the server's file.

choices.text: Encrypts DHCP so other PCs cannot read it
choices.why: DHCP stays in clear; snooping only filters it.

prompt: Match each DHCP message to how it travels in this lesson's captures.
hint: Who sends it, and to whom?

pairs.right: Server to client, proposing an address
Server to client, confirming the address
Client straight to the server, giving it back

right_distractors: Router to client, naming the gateway

prompt: pc1's lease started at 11:20:32, and its own lease file says `renew 2 2026/09/29 11:25:24`. How many seconds after the start is the renewal?
hint: Subtract the times.

prompt: An office pool holds 100 addresses, lent for one day. On Monday morning 105 PCs ask, one after another. What do the last five get?
hint: Every address in the pool is already lent.

choices.text: An address outside the range, chosen by the server
choices.why: The server lends from the range and nowhere else; the rest is kept for static use.

choices.text: No offer at all
choices.why: Right. Their DISCOVERs go unanswered, and many systems then fall back to 169.254.x.x.

choices.text: An address shared with another PC
choices.why: The server never lends one address twice at once.

choices.text: The same pool, with a shorter lease
choices.why: The lease length does not create addresses.

prompt: On r1, the ISC program that carries pc4's DHCP broadcasts across to srv is ___.
hint: Its name says DHCP and what it does.
